uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0834.explanation: Wine contains ethanol, which is oxidized by bacteria (Acetobacter) to acetic acid (vinegar). The conversion is oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0835.explanation: There are 4 structural isomers for C4H9Br: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0836.explanation: The document states, 'A single molecule of beryllium chloride (BeCl2) has a linear structure.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0837.explanation: Free radicals are stabilized by alkyl groups via hyperconjugation. Therefore, a tertiary radical is the most stable.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0838.explanation: Page 6 states, 'But beryllium is uncreative. It can only react above 600°C but the powder is much more reactive.' This implies it's less reactive than other Group 2 metals at lower temperatures.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0839.explanation: Synthetic detergents are typically sodium alkyl sulfates (ROSO3Na) or sodium alkyl sulfonates. RCOONa is the formula for soap (carboxylate salt).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0840.explanation: n-Butane (CH3CH2CH2CH3) has two types of hydrogens: terminal (methyl) and internal (methylene). Chlorination at C1 or C4 gives 1-chlorobutane, and at C2 or C3 gives 2-chlorobutane. Thus, only 2 monochlorinated products are formed.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0841.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point, density, etc.) but have opposite specific rotations (same magnitude, opposite sign). Therefore, they do NOT have the same specific rotation.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0842.explanation: Z (from German 'zusammen', meaning 'together') indicates the highest priority groups are on the same side. E ('entgegen', 'apart') indicates opposite sides.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0843.explanation: Diamond has a 3D tetrahedral network where each carbon is sp³ hybridized and covalently bonded to four other carbons with bond angles of 109.5°.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0844.explanation: The xanthoproteic test involves warming protein with concentrated nitric acid, which gives a yellow color due to nitration of aromatic amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan, phenylalanine).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0845.explanation: Page 23 states, 'All lower hydrides are colourless gases.' and 'The liquids have low boiling points due to weak intermolecular attraction.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0846.explanation: Isocyanides (R-NC) have a notoriously foul, penetrating odor, which makes the carbylamine test useful for detecting primary amines.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0847.explanation: Page 9 states: 'The value of half-life is independent of the amount of isotope (i.e. regardless of if we have 1 g or 1000 g of <sup>24</sup>Na the half-life is still 15 hrs)'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0848.explanation: Aniline reacts with bromine water to give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (white precipitate) because the amino group is strongly activating and ortho-para directing, leading to polybromination.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0849.explanation: Terminal alkynes form insoluble silver acetylides (white precipitate) with ammoniacal AgNO₃, distinguishing them from internal alkynes and alkenes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0850.explanation: n-Hexane is an alkane and does not react with concentrated H2SO4. Alkenes (1-butene) dissolve by protonation and subsequent reactions, ethers form oxonium salts, and aniline forms anilinium salts with acids.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0851.explanation: CH3CH2NH2 is ethylamine (common name) or ethanamine (IUPAC).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0852.explanation: Cyclopentanol (a secondary cyclic alcohol) undergoes oxidation to give cyclopentanone (a cyclic ketone).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0853.explanation: Steam distillation is ideal for isolating volatile, water-immiscible natural products like essential oils (eugenol, limonene) without decomposing them at high temperatures.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0854.explanation: n-Butyl bromide (CH3CH2CH2CH2Br) reacts with sodium hydrosulfide (NaSH) via SN2 to give n-butanethiol (CH3CH2CH2CH2SH). The SH- ion replaces the bromide.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0855.explanation: LiAlH₄ reduces ketones to secondary alcohols (R-CO-R' → R-CHOH-R'). Both NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ give the same alcohol products.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0856.explanation: 2-Methyl-2-butene (CH3-C(CH3)=CH-CH3) reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxide to give 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (or 3-bromo-2-methylbutane), which is a secondary alkyl bromide (the bromine is attached to a secondary carbon).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0857.explanation: Homolytic cleavage (symmetrical breaking) of a covalent bond gives each atom one electron from the shared pair, producing two free radicals.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0858.explanation: 2-methyl-2-pentanol is a tertiary alcohol; the carbon bearing OH has no hydrogen to lose, so no oxidation occurs.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0859.explanation: The correct order of bond lengths is single > double > triple. Option A correctly represents this as C-C (longest) > C=C (medium) > C≡C (shortest).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0860.explanation: Only pi electrons and lone pair electrons (unshared valence electrons) can be delocalized in resonance structures. Sigma bonds and atomic positions remain fixed.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0861.explanation: A glycoside is the acetal (or ketal) formed when the anomeric OH of a sugar is replaced by an alkoxy group. It is a sugar acetal.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0862.explanation: The common name for CH3-O-CH3 is dimethyl ether. The IUPAC name is methoxymethane.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0863.explanation: Ozonolysis of 2-butene (CH3CH=CHCH3) with reductive workup cleaves the double bond to give two molecules of acetaldehyde (ethanal). Oxidative workup would give acetic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0864.explanation: A mixed anhydride has two different acyl groups: acetic propanoic anhydride (CH3CO-O-COCH2CH3).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0865.explanation: n-butane boils at -0.5°C, just below freezing, making it a gas at room temperature.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0866.explanation: Acidic hydrolysis of a nitrile gives a carboxylic acid (R-C≡N + 2H2O → RCOOH + NH3). Basic hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0867.explanation: LiAlH₄ reduces nitriles to primary amines by adding four hydrogens across the triple bond, converting -C≡N to -CH₂NH₂.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0868.explanation: n-Octane (straight-chain alkane) has the lowest octane number among C8 isomers because straight-chain alkanes knock the most. Branched alkanes have higher octane numbers.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0869.explanation: Phenols react with neutral FeCl₃ to form colored complexes, often violet, purple, blue, or green, depending on the phenol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0870.explanation: A high Rf value means the compound traveled almost as far as the solvent front, indicating weak adsorption to the stationary phase and high solubility in the mobile phase (nonpolar character).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0871.explanation: Alkenes undergo addition reactions because the π bond (which is weaker) is broken, and two new σ bonds are formed. The energy released from forming σ bonds is greater than the energy required to break the π bond, making the reaction thermodynamically favorable.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0872.explanation: 2-Propanol (isopropyl alcohol) reacts with KBr and concentrated H2SO4 (generating HBr in situ) to give 2-bromopropane (isopropyl bromide) via nucleophilic substitution. The bromide replaces the OH group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0873.explanation: Fischer esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H2SO4) produces an ester and water.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0874.explanation: The suffix identifies the primary functional group present (e.g., -ol for alcohols, -one for ketones).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0875.explanation: This requires a tie-breaker rule (more substituents).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0876.explanation: Secondary amines react with HNO₂ to form N-nitrosoamines (R₂N-N=O), which are usually yellow oils and are potent carcinogens.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0877.explanation: Acetone (CH3-CO-CH3) has 9 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond. The sigma bonds are: 6 C-H bonds, 2 C-C bonds, and 1 C-O sigma bond. The pi bond is the C=O pi bond.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0878.explanation: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is a symmetric tetrahedral molecule, and the bond dipoles cancel out, giving it a net dipole moment of zero. The other compounds are asymmetric and have a net dipole moment.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0879.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are relatively strong intermolecular forces, but they are much weaker than covalent bonds. Their bond strength typically falls in the range of 5-10 kcal/mol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0880.explanation: All low molecular weight amines (methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine) are soluble in water because they can form hydrogen bonds with water. Higher molecular weight amines are less soluble.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0881.explanation: Tert-butyl alcohol ((CH3)3COH) is most resistant to oxidation because it is a tertiary alcohol with no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the OH group. Primary and secondary alcohols can be oxidized.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0882.explanation: In an epoxide (three-membered cyclic ether), the carbon atoms are sp3 hybridized, but the bond angles are approximately 60°, causing significant ring strain.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0883.explanation: The solvent is butane, a nonpolar alkane. The solute with the greatest solubility will be the most nonpolar compound. (CH3)3CH (isobutane, an alkane) is nonpolar and will be most soluble. Methanol, methylamine, and dimethyl ether are polar.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0884.explanation: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-butanol follows Zaitsev's rule, giving the more substituted alkene as the major product. 2-Butene (CH3CH=CHCH3) is the more substituted and major product, with 1-butene as the minor product.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0885.explanation: The double helix of DNA is held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A=T and G≡C).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0886.explanation: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the electron cloud is displaced toward chlorine, creating a partial negative charge on Cl and partial positive on H.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0887.explanation: Page 4 explains that beryllium is an exception because 'Its electrons are not well shielded from its nucleus.' This leads to a small ionic radius and high polarizing power.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0888.explanation: Page 6 states, '✓ Lithium show anomalous behavior due to its small ionic size and high charge.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0889.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation (H₂/Pd, Pt, or Ni) saturates the double bond, converting 2‑butene to butane.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0891.explanation: 2‑Butyne (CH₃C≡CCH₃) has two methyl groups attached to the triple bond → dimethylacetylene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0892.explanation: The prefix contains all the details regarding branches or groups that are not part of the parent chain.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0893.explanation: CH2=CH-CH2OH is allyl alcohol; the IUPAC name is prop-2-en-1-ol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0894.explanation: Eicosane is the name for a 20-carbon chain.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0895.explanation: Boiling points increase with molecular weight. Butane (C4H10) has the highest molecular weight, followed by propane (C3H8), then ethane (C2H6). Therefore, butane has the highest boiling point.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0896.explanation: C₆₀ is named buckminsterfullerene after Buckminster Fuller, the architect who designed geodesic domes, because the molecule has a similar soccer-ball shape.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0897.explanation: Steam distillation allows volatile compounds to be distilled at temperatures below their normal boiling points, making it suitable for heat-sensitive natural products like essential oils.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0898.explanation: A single-headed curved arrow (fishhook) indicates the movement of a single electron, typically in radical reaction mechanisms.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0899.explanation: sp hybridization mixes one s and one p orbital, so the s-character is 1/2 = 50%.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0900.explanation: Alkynes contain π bonds (electron‑rich) and undergo electrophilic addition; alkanes have only σ bonds and need free‑radical conditions.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0901.explanation: Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because addition would destroy the delocalized π electron system (aromatic stabilization energy). Substitution preserves the aromatic ring.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0902.explanation: Markovnikov addition of water: H adds to the less substituted carbon, OH adds to the tertiary carbon, giving tert‑butyl alcohol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0903.explanation: The carbon atoms in a C=C double bond are sp2 hybridized. Each carbon has three sigma bonds (one to the other carbon and two to other atoms) and one unhybridized p-orbital forming a pi bond.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0905.explanation: Acetamide (CH3CONH2) is reduced by LiAlH4 to ethylamine (CH3CH2NH2). The carbonyl group is reduced to a methylene group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0906.explanation: SN1 reactions are favored by tertiary alkyl halides because they form the most stable carbocation intermediates. tert-Butyl chloride forms a tertiary carbocation, which is the most stable.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0907.explanation: Tetra- is used for four identical groups (e.g., tetramethyl).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0908.explanation: sec-Butyl chloride (CH3-CHCl-CH2-CH3) has a chiral center at C2 (attached to Cl, H, CH3, and CH2CH3), making it optically active. The other isomers lack a chiral center.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0909.explanation: Ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol) is used in antifreeze/coolant and as a monomer for polyester fibers.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0910.explanation: In the acid-catalyzed hydration of ethylene, the electrophile H+ (from H2SO4) attacks the double bond first, forming a carbocation intermediate. Then water (not HO–) attacks the carbocation.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0911.explanation: The carbonyl oxygen in carboxylic acids is sp2 hybridized, similar to other carbonyl compounds. It forms a sigma bond with carbon and has two lone pairs in sp2 orbitals.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0912.explanation: Formaldehyde (H2C=O) reacts with Grignard reagent (R-MgX) to give a primary alcohol (R-CH2OH) after workup, adding one carbon.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0913.explanation: The Hunsdiecker reaction is the decarboxylation of silver carboxylates with halogens (Br2) to form alkyl halides. Silver acetate with Br2 gives methyl bromide.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0914.explanation: Page 10 states, 'Ionic character in the chlorides increases down the group.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0915.explanation: Characteristic reactions of aromatic hydrocarbons (electrophilic aromatic substitution) are initiated by electrophiles (electron-poor species that attack the electron-rich benzene ring).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0916.explanation: n-Propylmagnesium bromide (CH3CH2CH2MgBr) reacts with CO2 to form a carboxylate salt, which upon acid hydrolysis gives butanoic acid (CH3CH2CH2COOH). The Grignard reagent adds to CO2 to form a carboxylic acid with one more carbon.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0917.explanation: FeCl3 acts as a Lewis acid catalyst in the chlorination of benzene. It reacts with Cl2 to form Cl+ (or a complex that is a better electrophile), which is then attacked by benzene's π electrons.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0918.explanation: Propyne can be prepared by the reaction of sodium acetylide (NaC≡CH) with methyl chloride (CH3Cl) via nucleophilic substitution. This is an alkylation of acetylide ion.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0919.explanation: CH3NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH → CH3NC + 3KCl + 3H2O. Methyl isocyanide has a very unpleasant odor.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0920.explanation: Chlorobenzene is unaffected by boiling aqueous NaOH because the C-Cl bond in aryl halides is strong and unreactive toward nucleophilic substitution (due to resonance stabilization). Chloroethane (alkyl halide) would hydrolyze, acetaldehyde would undergo aldol reactions, and ethyl acetate would hydrolyze.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0921.explanation: Alkyl tosylates (R-OTs) are excellent leaving groups in SN2 reactions; tosylate is the leaving group in the Williamson synthesis when tosylates are used instead of halides.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0922.explanation: Acid-catalyzed hydration of 2-methyl-2-pentene ((CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3) follows Markovnikov's rule. Water adds to give the more substituted alcohol, with OH going to the more substituted carbon (C2), forming 2-methyl-2-pentanol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0923.explanation: At the anode, carboxylate ions lose electrons and decarboxylate, producing CO2 and alkyl radicals that couple.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0924.explanation: In cyclic alcohols, the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group is automatically C1.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0925.explanation: Cinnamaldehyde is prepared by the condensation of benzaldehyde with acetaldehyde in the presence of NaOH (crossed aldol condensation followed by dehydration).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0926.explanation: Phenol is used as an antiseptic and disinfectant. It was historically used by Joseph Lister as a surgical antiseptic.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0927.explanation: Optical isomers (enantiomers) have identical physical and chemical properties except for their interaction with plane-polarized light. They are distinguished by their direction of rotation using a polarimeter.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0928.explanation: Sucrose will not give a red precipitate of Cu2O with Benedict's solution because it is a non-reducing sugar. Maltose, glucose, and fructose are reducing sugars and give the positive test.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0929.explanation: Benzotrichloride (C6H5CCl3) on hydrolysis gives benzoic acid (C6H5COOH). The three chlorine atoms on the same carbon are hydrolyzed to form the carboxylic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0930.explanation: Benzene is immiscible with water, but it forms the upper layer (less dense than water, density ~0.88 g/mL), not the lower layer. The other statements are true.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0931.explanation: Etard's reaction is the oxidation of toluene (or other alkylbenzenes) with chromyl chloride (CrO2Cl2) to give benzaldehyde. It is a selective oxidation that stops at the aldehyde stage.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0932.explanation: Zaitsev's rule: the most substituted (more stable) alkene is the major product in elimination reactions like dehydrohalogenation and dehydration.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0933.explanation: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol (R-CHOH-R') removes two hydrogens to form a ketone (R-CO-R').

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0934.explanation: Primary amines react with Hinsberg reagent to form sulfonamides that are soluble in aqueous NaOH due to the acidic N-H proton. Secondary amines give sulfonamides that are insoluble in NaOH. Tertiary amines do not react.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0935.explanation: CH3COOCH2CH3 + CH3NH2 → CH3CONHCH3 + CH3CH2OH. Aminolysis gives N-methylacetamide (secondary amide) and ethanol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0936.explanation: Ethanol heated with concentrated H2SO4 at 140°C undergoes intermolecular dehydration to form diethyl ether (CH3CH2OCH2CH3).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0937.explanation: Triacylglycerols with low melting points (oils) are composed of unsaturated fatty acids, not saturated fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids cause higher melting points (fats).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0939.explanation: Page 9 explains: 'This is true for the metals in the lower half of the group where the metal ions are big and have a low charge density.' This allows the formation of more complicated oxides to release more energy, making the system more energetically stable.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0940.explanation: 1-Butanamine is the IUPAC name (common name: butylamine). The suffix '-amine' indicates the amino group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0941.explanation: Zaitsev’s rule (also called Saytzeff’s rule) states that the most substituted alkene is the major elimination product.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0942.explanation: Page 12 states: 'Unlike the group 1 metals which possess solid hydrogencarbonates, the hydrogencarbonates of group 2 metals only exist in solution.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0943.explanation: In homolytic fission, the bond breaks evenly, with each carbon atom retaining one electron from the bond, forming two free radicals.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0944.explanation: Aldehyde has higher priority in this specific naming context for benzaldehyde derivatives, so -CHO is the suffix, and -COOH is the prefix 'carboxy-'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0945.explanation: Page 7 states: 'In a nuclear reaction, the sum of the mass number and the atomic number on both sides of the equation must be the same.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0946.explanation: 2-Butene (CH3CH=CHCH3) can exist as cis and trans isomers because each carbon of the double bond has a methyl group and a hydrogen atom. 1-Butene has CH2 at one end, cyclopropane is a ring, and acetone has no C=C.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0947.explanation: The chain is 4 carbons with a double bond between C2 and C3 and OH on C1. Numbering prioritizes the OH, so 2-buten-1-ol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0948.explanation: 1-Butyne (terminal alkyne, HC≡C-CH2-CH3) reacts with ammoniacal silver nitrate to form a white precipitate (silver acetylide). Alkenes (1-butene, 2-butene) and internal alkynes (2-butyne) do not react.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0949.explanation: Alkanes are insoluble in water, so solubility is not used for separation; fractional distillation uses boiling points.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0950.explanation: The total pressure equals the sum of the vapor pressures of water and the organic components (aqueous tension). When this sum equals atmospheric pressure, boiling occurs at a lower temperature than the normal boiling point of the organic compound.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0951.explanation: γ-Butyrolactone is a 5-membered cyclic ester (lactone). Caprolactam is a cyclic amide (lactam).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0952.explanation: 2-Butene (CH3CH=CHCH3) is a symmetrical alkene. Addition of HBr across the double bond gives 2-bromobutane (CH3CHBrCH2CH3). Both carbons of the double bond are equivalent, so only one product is formed.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0953.explanation: Lucas reagent is a mixture of concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl2. It is used to differentiate between primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols based on the rate of formation of an insoluble alkyl chloride.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0954.explanation: The n+1 rule: a proton with n equivalent neighboring protons is split into (n+1) peaks (e.g., a triplet with two neighbors).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0955.explanation: Page 13 states: 'Solubility trend is due to the high enthalpy of solvation of the smaller Be<sup>2+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0956.explanation: C₆₀ has a shape resembling a soccer ball, known as a truncated icosahedron, consisting of 60 carbon atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0957.explanation: Unsymmetrical anhydrides are named by citing the two acids alphabetically: ethanoic methanoic anhydride (common: acetic formic anhydride).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0958.explanation: NH2- is the leaving group, but because it is a very poor leaving group, amides are the least reactive derivatives. Hydrolysis requires harsh conditions.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0959.explanation: Ethylene oxide undergoes acid-catalyzed hydrolysis to yield ethylene glycol (HOCH2CH2OH, 1,2-ethanediol). The epoxide ring is opened by water.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0960.explanation: Numbering starts from the end closer to either the double or triple bond (the first site of unsaturation).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0961.explanation: Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs because they are closer to the nucleus and occupy more space, affecting bond angles and molecular shape.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0962.explanation: Acidification of the extract releases H₂S, which reacts with lead acetate to form black lead sulfide (PbS) precipitate.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0963.explanation: Diazonium salts are formed by the reaction of nitrous acid (HNO2) with primary aromatic amines (e.g., aniline) at low temperatures. Primary aliphatic amines give alcohols with nitrogen gas.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0964.explanation: A perfect tetrahedron has bond angles of 109.5°, as observed in methane and other sp³ hybridized centers with no lone pairs.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0965.explanation: Pt and Pd catalysts hydrogenate alkenes at room temperature, while Ni requires 250-300°C.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0966.explanation: 1,4-Dioxane is a 6-membered cyclic diether with oxygen atoms at positions 1 and 4. It is a common solvent.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0967.explanation: Alkynes decolorize Br2 and cold KMnO4 (addition reactions), and terminal alkynes also precipitate with AgNO3/NH3. So they give positive tests.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0968.explanation: 2,4-Hexadiene (CH3CH=CH-CH=CHCH3) has double bonds at C2 and C4 with one single bond between them (C2-C3-C4). The double bonds are separated by one single bond, making it a conjugated diene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0969.explanation: The order of increasing stability for dienes is: cumulated dienes (1,2-pentadiene) < isolated dienes (1,4-pentadiene) < conjugated cis dienes (cis-1,3-pentadiene) < conjugated trans dienes (trans-1,3-pentadiene). Conjugated dienes are stabilized by resonance, and trans isomers are more stable than cis.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0970.explanation: The document states that beryllium has a 'Small ionic radius – representing very dense centre of positive charge and high polarizing power.' A small ionic radius and high charge density lead to high polarizing power. Options A and B describe characteristics opposite to beryllium's. Option D is incorrect; its compounds are more covalent than ionic.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0971.explanation: Both are C₄H₆ alkynes differing only in the position of the triple bond (terminal vs internal).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0972.explanation: Propionamide (CH3CH2CONH2) is an amide and is a very weak base; it does not form salts with dilute HCl. Amines (primary, secondary, tertiary) are basic and form salts with HCl.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0973.explanation: For dehydration of an amide to a nitrile, the amide must be primary (CONH2). Secondary and tertiary amides cannot be dehydrated to nitriles because they lack the necessary N-H hydrogens to eliminate water.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0974.explanation: The rate of an SN1 reaction depends only on the concentration of the alkyl halide (and factors affecting carbocation formation like the nature of the alkyl halide and leaving group). The concentration of the nucleophile does not affect the rate because the nucleophile is not involved in the rate-determining step.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0975.explanation: Addition of excess HBr (2 equivalents) to 1-hexyne (CH≡C-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3) gives 2,2-dibromohexane. The first equivalent adds (Markovnikov) to give 2-bromo-1-hexene, and the second equivalent adds to give the geminal dibromide with both bromines on the same carbon.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0976.explanation: Page 10 states: 'With the exception of lithium which reacts slowly, group 1 metals react violently with water to give the corresponding hydroxide and liberate hydrogen gas.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0977.explanation: The Williamson synthesis works best with primary alkyl halides or methyl halides via SN2. Tertiary halides undergo elimination instead.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0978.explanation: 1,5-Octadiene has double bonds at C1 and C5, which are separated by more than one single bond (C1=C2-C3-C4-C5=C6). The double bonds are not adjacent or conjugated, making it an isolated diene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0979.explanation: mCPBA (meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid) epoxidizes cyclohexene to cyclohexene oxide (1,2-epoxycyclohexane).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0980.explanation: A meso form is an achiral molecule that contains chiral centers. Achiral molecules have superimposable mirror images, do not exhibit optical activity, and do not have enantiomers (meso compounds are their own mirror image).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0981.explanation: With 3 chiral centers, the number of stereoisomers is 2^n = 2^3 = 8 stereoisomers (4 pairs of enantiomers).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0982.explanation: Page 11 states, 'The ease of decomposition decreases down the group.' This means it becomes harder to decompose them as you go down the group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0983.explanation: In aqueous solution, nucleophilicity follows the order I- > Br- > Cl- > F- (for halides). Iodide is the most polarizable and therefore the strongest nucleophile among halides in water.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0984.explanation: Partial hydrogenation (e.g., Lindlar) converts sp‑hybridized alkyne carbons to sp²‑hybridized alkene carbons.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0985.explanation: Page 3 states, 'Their oxides and hydroxides are basic,' making option C incorrect. The other options are listed as characteristics of Group II metals.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0986.explanation: Clemmensen reduction (amalgamated zinc + concentrated HCl) reduces aldehydes and ketones to alkanes (R₂C=O → R₂CH₂) under acidic conditions.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0987.explanation: 1,2,3-propanetriol is a trihydric alcohol commonly known as glycerol. It is the backbone of fats.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0988.explanation: Rf values are characteristic for a given compound under specific conditions (solvent system, stationary phase, temperature) and can be used for identification by comparison with standards.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0989.explanation: RCOCl + R'NH2 → RCONHR' + HCl. The product is a secondary amide (N-substituted amide).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0990.explanation: Propyne (methylacetylene) when passed through a hot iron tube at 400°C undergoes trimerization to give mesitylene (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0991.explanation: Dehydration gives a mixture of cis and trans-2-butene, with the more stable trans isomer predominating over cis, plus a small amount of 1-butene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0992.explanation: Isopropyl alcohol (secondary alcohol) is oxidized to acetone using an oxidizing agent like sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid (Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0993.explanation: Aniline reacts with acetyl chloride (acetylation), acetic anhydride (acetylation), and nitrous acid (diazotization). Ammonia does not react with aniline under normal conditions.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0994.explanation: The condenser is a cooling jacket that condenses the hot vapor back into liquid, which then collects in the receiving flask.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0995.explanation: Acid protonates the alkene, generating a carbocation that is attacked by water, followed by deprotonation to give the alcohol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0996.explanation: Lucas test is used to distinguish between primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols based on their reactivity with HCl/ZnCl2. Tertiary alcohols react immediately, secondary within 5-10 minutes, and primary do not react at room temperature.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0997.explanation: sp³ hybridization mixes one s and three p orbitals, so the s-character is 1/4 = 25%. sp² has 33%, sp has 50%.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0998.explanation: Increased conjugation lowers the HOMO-LUMO gap, causing absorption at longer wavelengths (higher λmax, bathochromic shift).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-0999.explanation: In TLC, the solvent rises through the adsorbent layer (silica gel or alumina) by capillary action, carrying the sample components with it at different rates based on their adsorption affinities.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1000.explanation: Aryl halides are less reactive toward nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides because the C-X bond has partial double bond character due to resonance (lone pair on halogen delocalized into the ring), making it stronger and less susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1001.explanation: Digestion of proteins involves the cleavage of peptide linkages (amide bonds) by enzymes (proteases) to break the protein down into smaller peptides and amino acids.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1002.explanation: Alcohols react with sodium metal to release hydrogen gas (effervescence), indicating the presence of a free -OH group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1003.explanation: Page 5, in the 'Units of radioactivity' table, the 'Definition' for 'Becquerel' is '1 disintegration per second (dps)'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1004.explanation: Oxirane (three-membered cyclic ether) is commonly called ethylene oxide. It is an important industrial intermediate.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1005.explanation: When 2-iodohexane is heated in ethanol (a polar protic solvent, weak nucleophile, weak base), it undergoes solvolysis via SN1 and elimination via E1. The weak nucleophile/base and formation of a carbocation intermediate favor both SN1 and E1.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1006.explanation: The compound is butan-2-ol, which is the same as 2-butanol. Both are acceptable IUPAC names (the number can be placed before or after the root).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1007.explanation: 2-methyl-2-propanol has the OH carbon bonded to three alkyl groups (methyl groups), making it a tertiary alcohol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1008.explanation: Higher s-character (sp > sp² > sp³) means electrons are held closer to the nucleus, making the carbon more electronegative.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1009.explanation: An octane number of 90 means the fuel has the same knocking characteristics as a mixture containing 90% isooctane and 10% n-heptane. This corresponds to 10% heptane + 90% isooctane.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1010.explanation: Ethylene glycol is commonly used as an antifreeze in automotive cooling systems due to its ability to lower the freezing point of water.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1011.explanation: Under basic conditions, the ring-opening of epoxides is SN2-like. The nucleophile attacks the less hindered (less substituted) carbon of the epoxide.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1012.explanation: Ammonia attacks the less substituted carbon of an epoxide, opening the ring to form an amino alcohol (NH2-CH2-CH2-OH from ethylene oxide).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1013.explanation: TLC is a quick, simple, and inexpensive technique for monitoring reaction progress, checking purity, and identifying compounds by comparison with standards.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1014.explanation: The compound is a secondary aromatic amine: N-methylaniline. The 'N' indicates the methyl is attached to nitrogen, not the ring.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1015.explanation: 1-Butyne (C4H6, CH≡C-CH2-CH3) reacts with bromine (unsaturation), forms precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO3 (terminal alkyne), and hydration gives 2-butanone (CH3-CO-CH2CH3). 2-Butyne (internal alkyne) does not give AgNO3 precipitate.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1016.explanation: Page 8 states, 'Potassium, rubidium and caesium form superoxides O₂⁻'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1017.explanation: In gas chromatography, the stationary phase is usually a high-boiling liquid (e.g., polysiloxane) coated on an inert solid support inside a capillary column.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1018.explanation: C4H8O is an aldehyde or ketone. No reaction with Na or PCl5 means it is not an alcohol. Reducing alkaline Cu(II) salt (Fehling's test) indicates an aliphatic aldehyde. So compound (A) is an aldehyde.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1019.explanation: Phenol has the most acidic proton among the options because the phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance. Thiols are more acidic than alcohols, but phenols are more acidic than thiols. Ethers have no acidic proton.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1020.explanation: The ethyl group ($CH_3CH_2-$) is commonly abbreviated as Et.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1021.explanation: The oxygen in ethers is sp3 hybridized with a bond angle of approximately 112° (slightly larger than the tetrahedral angle due to lone pair repulsion).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1022.explanation: The compound is a secondary aromatic amine: N-methylaniline. The 'N' indicates the methyl is attached to nitrogen, not the ring.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1023.explanation: Tertiary aliphatic amines lack an N-H bond, so they simply form soluble ammonium salts with the acid and do not undergo nitrosation under these conditions.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1024.explanation: First HBr gives CH₂=CHBr; the second HBr adds Markovnikov to give CH₃CHBr₂ (1,1‑dibromoethane).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1025.explanation: A six-carbon chain with two methyl groups on carbon 2 is 2,2-dimethylbutane.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1026.explanation: In the gas phase or nonpolar solvents, the basicity order is: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3. In aqueous solution, dimethylamine is the most basic due to a balance of inductive effects and solvation. Methyl groups are electron-donating, increasing basicity, but steric hindrance and solvation affect higher alkylamines.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1027.explanation: Hydrazones are formed by reaction of aldehydes or ketones with hydrazine (NH₂NH₂), giving R₂C=N-NH₂.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1028.explanation: Propanone is the IUPAC name for CH₃COCH₃ (common name: acetone). The suffix for ketones is '-one'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1029.explanation: Four bonding pairs and zero lone pairs (e.g., CH₄) give a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of 109.5°.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1030.explanation: Page 19 shows a trend of 'Decreasing stability' and 'Decreasing Basicity' when moving from CO₂ down to PbO₂. However, this contradicts the typical trend where metallic character increases down a group, leading to increased basicity of oxides. Given that CO₂ is acidic and PbO₂ (and GeO₂, SnO₂) are amphoteric (react with both acids and bases), the oxides generally become *less acidic* and therefore *more basic* down the group. The 'Decreasing Basicity' label on the slide likely refers to the *acidic* character or is a typo. The correct chemical trend is increasing basicity.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1031.explanation: Propanenitrile (CH3CH2CN) undergoes acid-hydrolysis to give propionic acid (CH3CH2COOH). The nitrile is hydrolyzed to the corresponding carboxylic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1032.explanation: Chlorobenzene is prepared by electrophilic aromatic substitution of benzene with chlorine in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst like FeCl3. UV light causes free radical addition to give benzene hexachloride, not chlorobenzene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1033.explanation: 1-Methoxypropane (an ether) has the lowest boiling point because it cannot form hydrogen bonds (no O-H group). The alcohols (1-butanol, 2-butanol, and 1,1-dimethylethanol) can all form hydrogen bonds and have higher boiling points.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1034.explanation: Marsh gas is primarily composed of methane (CH4), which is produced by the decomposition of organic matter in swamps and marshes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1035.explanation: Cold, alkaline KMnO4 (or OsO4) adds two OH groups across the double bond via syn addition, forming a vicinal diol (glycol). The purple color disappears, turning brown (MnO2).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1036.explanation: Markovnikov addition of water followed by tautomerization of the enol gives a methyl ketone: butanone (CH₃CH₂COCH₃).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1037.explanation: Acetone reacts with HCN to form acetone cyanohydrin, an important intermediate in the production of methyl methacrylate.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1038.explanation: Diamond has a density of about 3.5 g/cm³ due to its tightly packed tetrahedral lattice, making it denser than graphite.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1039.explanation: Formaldehyde (H2CO) has no alkyl group; reaction with RMgX gives R-CH2OH, a primary alcohol with one additional carbon.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1040.explanation: Page 8 explicitly states, 'Basicity increases down the Gp.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1041.explanation: Nitration of nitrobenzene gives m-dinitrobenzene (1,3-dinitrobenzene) because the nitro group is a meta director.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1042.explanation: Glucose is a monosaccharide, not a disaccharide. It is a reducing sugar, exists in pyranose form, and has multiple hydroxyl groups (polyalcohol).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1043.explanation: For C8H10, the possible aromatic isomers include ethylbenzene and the three xylene isomers (o-, m-, p-xylene), giving a total of 4 isomers.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1044.explanation: Ethylene glycol (HOCH2CH2OH) on oxidation with hot acidic KMnO4 (strong oxidation) gives formic acid (HCOOH). The glycol is cleaved at the C-C bond, and each carbon is oxidized to formic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1045.explanation: Alkynes, which have triple bonds, use the suffix -yne.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1046.explanation: Bromine in CCl4 tests for unsaturation. Butane is an alkane (saturated hydrocarbon) and will not react with bromine in CCl4, giving a negative test (no decolorization). Alkenes (2-butene, 1,3-butadiene) and alkynes (2-butyne) will decolorize the bromine solution.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1047.explanation: Methanol is synthesized from synthesis gas (CO + 2H2) at high temperature (400°C) and pressure (200 atm) over metal catalysts.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1048.explanation: Both double and triple bonds are suffixes, with -ene coming before -yne alphabetically (e.g., hex-3-en-1-yne). Numbering gives the first multiple bond the lowest number.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1049.explanation: Glucose exists predominantly as a cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose form), but in solution it is in equilibrium with the open-chain aldehyde form. It is this open-chain form that gives aldehyde reactions.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1050.explanation: Alkenes and alkynes are more reactive than alkanes because they contain pi bonds (electron-rich regions) that can be attacked by electrophiles. Pi bonds are weaker and more accessible than sigma bonds.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1051.explanation: Organic chemistry is fundamental to drug discovery and development, including antibiotics, vaccines, and many pharmaceutical agents.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1052.explanation: AlCl3 is a Lewis acid and an electrophile because it has an incomplete octet and accepts electron pairs. The other options (NH3, HSO3-, HO-) have lone pairs and are nucleophiles.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1053.explanation: LiAlH4 reduces esters to primary alcohols: RCOOR' → RCH2OH + R'OH. Both the acyl and alkoxy parts become alcohols.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1054.explanation: Dehydration of 2-butanol follows Zaitsev's rule to give the more substituted alkene, 2-butene (a mixture of cis/trans).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1055.explanation: Neoprene is a synthetic rubber made by polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene, CH2=C(Cl)-CH=CH2).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1056.explanation: All statements are correct: A larger Ka means a stronger acid (more dissociation). A small pKa corresponds to a large Ka (since pKa = -log Ka). And a smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1057.explanation: 1-butanol is a straight-chain primary alcohol with the most surface area for intermolecular hydrogen bonding, giving a higher boiling point than branched isomers.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1058.explanation: When a ketone is not the highest priority, it is named as a prefix using 'oxo-'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1059.explanation: Vitalism was the belief that organic compounds required a 'vital force' from living organisms and could not be synthesized artificially.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1060.explanation: Aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde are oxidized to benzoic acid under alkaline KMnO₄ conditions. They are less easily oxidized than aliphatic aldehydes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1061.explanation: A hemiacetal has both an -OH and an -OR group on the same carbon, formed from the addition of one alcohol molecule to an aldehyde.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1062.explanation: Bond length decreases with increasing bond order. A triple bond is the shortest, followed by a double bond, and a single bond is the longest. Therefore, the increasing order is triple < double < single.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1063.explanation: In 1,3-butadiene, resonance delocalization gives the central C2-C3 bond partial double bond character (bond order >1), making it shorter than a typical single bond.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1064.explanation: Aniline (primary amine) with chloroform and alcoholic KOH gives phenylisocyanide (phenyl carbylamine), which has a foul smell. This is the carbylamine test for primary amines.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1065.explanation: Glycine exists as a zwitterion (NH3+CH2COO-) in aqueous solution, which is neutral overall. The positive and negative charges balance each other.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1066.explanation: Carboxylic acid has higher priority, so -NH₂ is a substituent (prefix 'amino-').

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1067.explanation: Catenation is the unique property of carbon atoms to form long chains and rings by bonding with other carbon atoms. This is the basis for the vast number and diversity of organic compounds.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1068.explanation: Page 9 defines half-life as 'the time it takes to lose half its radioactivity'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1069.explanation: The C-C bond length in graphite is 1.42 Å, which is shorter than the C-C single bond in diamond (1.54 Å) and has partial double bond character due to delocalization.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1070.explanation: p-Nitrotoluene has two directing groups: the methyl group (ortho-para director, activating) and the nitro group (meta director, deactivating). The methyl group dominates, directing incoming electrophile to ortho (position 2) to the methyl group, giving 2-chloro-4-nitrotoluene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1071.explanation: Ethanol and secondary alcohols with a methyl group on the carbinol carbon (CH3CHOH-R) give the iodoform test. Ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde, which gives iodoform.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1072.explanation: Benzenediazonium chloride is prepared from aniline by diazotization using sodium nitrite (NaNO2) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) at 0-5°C.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1073.explanation: According to page 3, the general electronic configuration for atoms of elements in the P-block is ns²npᵐ, where 'm' typically ranges from 1 to 6.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1074.explanation: Esters can be hydrolyzed under both basic conditions (saponification, irreversible) and acidic conditions (reversible Fischer esterification reverse reaction). Both methods are effective.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1075.explanation: Silver oxide catalyzes the reaction of alcohols with alkyl halides to form ethers, often used for sensitive compounds like carbohydrates.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1076.explanation: The inductive effect is a permanent effect where a non-polar bond becomes polarized due to the electron-withdrawing or electron-donating nature of an adjacent group, transmitted through sigma bonds.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1077.explanation: A carbon-carbon triple bond consists of one sigma bond (2 electrons) and two pi bonds (4 electrons), totaling 6 electrons involved in the triple bond.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1078.explanation: Boiling points increase with increasing molecular weight and hydrogen bonding capability. Compound (3) has the lowest boiling point, followed by (2), then (1) with the highest.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1079.explanation: The acid-catalyzed dehydration of alcohols to form ethers also involves formation of a carbocation (carbonium ion) intermediate. Protonation of the alcohol is followed by nucleophilic attack of another alcohol molecule on the carbocation.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1080.explanation: Aniline diazotizes to benzenediazonium chloride when treated with ice-cold nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl at 0-5°C). Aniline is a weak base (not acid), nitration requires protection of the amino group, and the bleaching powder test is for phenols.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1081.explanation: TLC separates compounds based on their differential adsorption to the stationary phase; Rf = distance compound / distance solvent front.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1082.explanation: The C=O bond is shorter (1.23 Å vs 1.34 Å), stronger (178 kcal/mol vs 146 kcal/mol), and more polar than a C=C bond due to the higher electronegativity of oxygen.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1083.explanation: Iodide (I-) is the best nucleophile in water among the options. CH3SCH3 and CH3OCH3 are neutral and less nucleophilic than anions. Cl- is a weaker nucleophile than I- in water due to its smaller size and less polarizability.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1084.explanation: ZnCl2 coordinates with the oxygen of the alcohol, making the OH a better leaving group and facilitating the SN1 reaction.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1085.explanation: The longest chain containing the triple bond has 4 carbons, numbered to give the triple bond the lowest number, so 1‑butyne.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1086.explanation: Ethers are stored in brown bottles to prevent exposure to light and air, which can cause oxidation to form explosive peroxides.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1087.explanation: Ethoxyethane (IUPAC), diethyl ether (common), and ethyl ether are all acceptable names for this solvent.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1088.explanation: Empirical formula mass of CH₂O = 30 g/mol. 180/30 = 6, so molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1089.explanation: 2,4,6-trimethylheptane (CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3) has no asymmetric centers. The carbons at positions 2, 4, and 6 each have two identical methyl groups, so they are not chiral.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1090.explanation: The 'Properties of radiation' table on page 4, under the 'β - Rays' column for 'Stopped by', states '1 cm of aluminium'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1091.explanation: Butanone (CH3CH2COCH3) does not give a positive iodoform test because it does not have the CH3CO- group. Ethanol (oxidized to acetaldehyde), propanone (acetone), and 2-propanol (oxidized to acetone) all have the CH3CO- or CH3CHOH- group and give positive tests.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1092.explanation: A triol is an alcohol with three -OH groups.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1093.explanation: Tertiary alcohols are often more soluble due to their more compact, spherical shape that disrupts water structure less, though miscibility varies.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1094.explanation: Acetone (CH3COCH3) reacts with methylmagnesium bromide (CH3MgBr) to give tert-butyl alcohol ((CH3)3COH) after hydrolysis. The Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetone.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1095.explanation: Chirality is the property of a molecule that makes it non-superimposable on its mirror image. If a molecule can be superimposed on its mirror image, it is achiral.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1096.explanation: 2-Methylpentane has a pentane parent chain (5 carbons) with one methyl substituent, giving a total of 6 carbon atoms. The formula for an alkane with 6 carbons is C6H14.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1097.explanation: SN2 reactions require unhindered alkyl halides; primary and methyl halides work best. Tertiary halides undergo elimination instead.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1098.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2, where n is the number of carbon atoms.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1099.explanation: Page 11 states that diamond is a 'non-conductor' of electricity. Options A, B, and D are all correct descriptions of diamond.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1100.explanation: Monochloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid because chlorine is electron-withdrawing, stabilizing the conjugate base. Acetic acid is stronger than propionic acid (alkyl groups are electron-donating). Trichloroacetic acid and formic acid are both stronger than acetic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1101.explanation: The electromeric effect is temporary and occurs only in multiple bonds (pi bonds) when a reagent approaches; the electrons return to original positions after the reagent is removed.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1102.explanation: Hofmann elimination converts an amine to an alkene via formation of a quaternary ammonium salt followed by treatment with base, giving the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1103.explanation: Ethanol reacts with sodium metal to form sodium ethoxide (CH3CH2ONa), which is an ionic compound (contains Na+ and CH3CH2O- ions). The other reactions give covalent products (ethyl chloride, ethyl bromide, etc.).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1104.explanation: Melting points of aldehydes and ketones generally increase with increasing molecular weight due to stronger van der Waals forces between larger molecules.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1105.explanation: The three atoms attached to the carbonyl carbon form a planar (trigonal planar) geometry, not nonplanar. The other statements are true: sp2 hybridization, 120° bond angles, and resonance structures.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1106.explanation: Concentrated H2SO4 is used as a catalyst/dehydrating agent in the nitration of benzene. It protonates HNO3 to generate the electrophile NO2+.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1107.explanation: The three-carbon chain with a terminal -COOH gives propanoic acid (common name: propionic acid).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1108.explanation: The first step in aldol condensation is the abstraction of an alpha hydrogen by a base to form an enolate anion. This enolate then attacks the carbonyl carbon of another molecule.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1109.explanation: Dicarboxylic acids have higher melting points than monocarboxylic acids of similar molecular weight because they can form more extensive hydrogen bonding networks (two -COOH groups) and have more symmetrical structures that pack better in the crystal lattice.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1110.explanation: Page 15 states, 'Group 1 metals are the only metals that form solid bicarbonates (hydrogenbicarbonates) except LiHCO₃ which exit only in solution'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1111.explanation: Page 5 explicitly states: '* Quality factor of: α ray is 20'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1112.explanation: Cyclohexanone (a ketone) is reduced by LiAlH4 or NaBH4 to cyclohexanol (an alcohol).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1113.explanation: 3-Hexyne (CH3CH2-C≡C-CH2CH3) on ozonolysis gives propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH) as the only product. Both carbons of the triple bond bear ethyl groups, which are oxidized to propanoic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1114.explanation: n-Butyl alcohol (1-butanol) has the highest boiling point among the options because it can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. The other compounds (ether, aldehyde, alkyl chloride) have only dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1115.explanation: In the Carius method, the sample is heated with fuming HNO₃ and AgNO₃ in a sealed tube; halogens precipitate as AgCl, AgBr, or AgI.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1116.explanation: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism in alkenes arises because the carbon-carbon double bond prevents free rotation. This restriction allows for different spatial arrangements of substituents.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1117.explanation: Chlorobenzene can be prepared from aniline via diazotization followed by Sandmeyer reaction with CuCl. Aniline → benzenediazonium chloride → chlorobenzene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1118.explanation: The parent name is derived specifically from the longest continuous carbon chain found in the molecule.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1119.explanation: Page 4, under the 'Properties' table, states that the 'Nature' of 'α - Rays' is 'Helium nuclei <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He (particles)'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1120.explanation: IUPAC name is ethanoic anhydride (common: acetic anhydride).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1121.explanation: Justus von Liebig developed the classical combustion method for determining carbon and hydrogen percentages in organic compounds.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1122.explanation: As molecular weight increases, boiling points increase steadily. Melting points also generally increase but not as smoothly; there is a zigzag pattern due to packing efficiency in the solid state, especially for alkanes with more than four carbons.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1123.explanation: The document states, 'Ionic character in the chlorides increases down the group.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1124.explanation: The electromeric effect is a temporary effect involving complete transfer of pi electrons to one atom of a multiple bond when an attacking reagent approaches.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1125.explanation: Methoxyethane (IUPAC) and ethyl methyl ether (common) are both correct. The smaller alkoxy group is named as prefix.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1126.explanation: Each carbon in a C=C double bond is sp2 hybridized, with trigonal planar geometry and a bond angle of approximately 120°.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1127.explanation: Fructose is a ketohexose (ketone group), not an aldohexose (aldehyde group). The other statements are true about aldohexoses.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1128.explanation: UV-Vis spectroscopy measures electronic transitions (π→π* and n→π*) in conjugated systems, indicating chromophores and extent of conjugation.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1129.explanation: Butanenitrile (butyronitrile) has the lowest boiling point because nitriles have weaker intermolecular forces (dipole-dipole) compared to alcohols and carboxylic acids (which have hydrogen bonding) and esters (which have dipole-dipole interactions but higher molecular weight).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1130.explanation: Partial hydrogenation converts sp-hybridized alkyne carbons to sp2-hybridized alkene carbons.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1131.explanation: Page 8 lists Spinthariscopes, scintillation counters, Geiger-Muller counters, cloude chambers, and bubble chambers as equipment. Mass spectrometers are not mentioned.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1132.explanation: Alkynes are reduced more readily than alkenes because they are more unsaturated and can adsorb more strongly onto the metal catalyst surface during hydrogenation, making the reaction faster.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1133.explanation: Fullerenes are used in photodynamic therapy for cancer treatment, where they generate reactive oxygen species upon light activation to kill cancer cells.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1134.explanation: Amides are the most stable of the carboxylic acid derivatives because they have the most stable resonance forms, with significant contribution from the resonance structure where the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, giving the C-N bond partial double bond character.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1135.explanation: Thionyl chloride (SOCl2) is the most common reagent for converting carboxylic acids to acid chlorides, producing SO2 and HCl as byproducts.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1136.explanation: Zwitterions have no net charge (overall neutral but with internal charges), high melting points (due to ionic interactions), and are soluble in water (polar).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1137.explanation: Page 7 describes the typical properties: 'Anomalous 1st row element – small size; high EN', '2nd row element much less EN than 1st row', and '3rd row element has higher EN (middle row anomaly)'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1138.explanation: A lactam is a cyclic amide formed by reaction of an -NH2 and -COOH group on the same molecule.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1139.explanation: The acid is butanoic acid (C4), the alcohol is methanol, so methyl butanoate (common: methyl butyrate).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1140.explanation: Terminal alkynes have pKa ≈ 25, which is much more acidic than alkanes (pKa ~50) and alkenes (pKa ~44) but less acidic than water (pKa 15.7) or alcohols.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1141.explanation: At room temperature, amines and carboxylic acids undergo an acid-base reaction to form a water-soluble ammonium carboxylate salt. Heating can convert this to an amide.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1142.explanation: Acetic anhydride reacts with ethanol (ethanal is a typo; it should be ethanol) to give ethyl acetate. Acetic anhydride + ethanol → ethyl acetate + acetic acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1143.explanation: In phospholipids, the glycerol is esterified with two fatty acids (at C1 and C2) and a phosphate at C3 (not the middle OH group, which is C2). The middle OH (C2) is esterified with a fatty acid, not phosphate.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1144.explanation: Page 23 provides the reaction: 'Na₂SO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + SO₂(g) + H₂O(l)'. Sulphur dioxide gas is liberated.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1145.explanation: Water has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. Lone pair repulsion compresses the bond angle to about 104.5°, giving a bent shape.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1146.explanation: CH₃CHO is acetaldehyde (common name) or ethanal (IUPAC). Formaldehyde is HCHO, propionaldehyde is CH₃CH₂CHO, benzaldehyde is C₆H₅CHO.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1147.explanation: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/CaCO3 with quinoline) hydrogenates alkynes to cis-alkenes without further reduction to alkanes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1148.explanation: For comparable molecular weights, boiling points increase in the order: alkanes < ethers < thiols < alcohols. This reflects increasing strength of intermolecular forces: van der Waals < dipole-dipole < dipole-dipole + weak H-bonding < strong H-bonding.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1149.explanation: NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols. Propanal is reduced to 1-propanol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1150.explanation: Thionyl chloride (SOCl2) replaces the -OH group of an alcohol with a chlorine atom, forming an alkyl chloride. The reaction is: ROH + SOCl2 → RCl + SO2 + HCl.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1151.explanation: After recrystallization, the solid crystals are collected by filtration (usually vacuum filtration) to separate them from the mother liquor containing impurities.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1152.explanation: Resorcinol (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) on distillation with zinc dust gives benzene (C6H6). The hydroxyl groups are reduced and removed.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1153.explanation: Catenation is the unique property of carbon atoms to bond covalently with each other to form long chains, rings, and branched structures, leading to millions of organic compounds.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1154.explanation: The molecule is 1-butene (CH3CH2CH=CH2). According to Markovnikov's rule, the H from HCl adds to C-1 (the terminal carbon) because it already has more hydrogens (two H atoms) compared to C-2 (one H atom).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1155.explanation: Page 7 mentions: 'Last element has higher EN than expected (Lanthanide contraction)'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1156.explanation: Lone pairs are regions of high electron density and act as nucleophiles (electron-pair donors) in many organic reactions, even if not always drawn.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1157.explanation: CH3CH2CN is propanenitrile (IUPAC) or ethyl cyanide (common). The carbon of the CN group is counted in the chain: propane + nitrile.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1158.explanation: Pi bonds are formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the plane of the molecule, giving electron density in two lobes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1159.explanation: In a chain reaction, the product of one step generates a reactive intermediate (like a free radical) that initiates the next step. This propagation continues until termination occurs.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1160.explanation: The longest chain is 4 carbons with a methyl on C3 and OH on C1, so 3-methyl-1-butanol.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1161.explanation: Alcohols are designated by the suffix '-ol' replacing the '-e' of the parent alkane.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1162.explanation: Ethers have no O-H bond, so they cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other (unlike alcohols). Only weak dipole-dipole and London forces exist, leading to lower boiling points.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1163.explanation: Tertiary amines (3°) do not react with acyl chlorides to form amides because they have no N-H hydrogen to be replaced by the acyl group. Ammonia, 1° and 2° amines all have N-H hydrogens and form amides.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1164.explanation: Alkenes are nonpolar hydrocarbons; they cannot hydrogen-bond with water and are insoluble in water but soluble in nonpolar organic solvents.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1165.explanation: In the electrophilic addition of HCl to propene, the H+ ion is the electrophile. It is electron-deficient and attacks the electron-rich double bond of the alkene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1166.explanation: Page 7 clearly states: 'In a nuclear reaction, the sum of the mass number and the atomic number on both sides of the equation must be the same.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1167.explanation: Bakelite is a thermosetting polymer made from phenol and formaldehyde. It is used as an adhesive and in electrical insulators. All statements are correct.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1168.explanation: Carboxylic acids react with NaHCO₃ to release CO₂ gas (effervescence), which turns limewater milky. This test is specific for free -COOH groups.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1169.explanation: Alkene stability increases with the number of alkyl substituents on the double bond (more substituted alkenes are more stable). 2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene is a disubstituted alkene, more stable than ethylene (unsubstituted), propylene (monosubstituted), and 2-butene (disubstituted but less substituted than 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1170.explanation: The cyano group (-CN) is electron-withdrawing by induction (-I effect) due to the high electronegativity of nitrogen.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1171.explanation: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen atoms. This is the definition of hydrocarbons.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1172.explanation: Since the boiling points differ by more than 100°C (60°C vs 189°C), simple distillation is sufficient to separate chloroform (lower bp) from aniline (higher bp).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1173.explanation: 2-Methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol, tertiary) reacts fastest with HBr because it forms the most stable tertiary carbocation. The reactivity order with HX is: tertiary > secondary > primary.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1174.explanation: n-Octane has the largest molecular weight (C8H18) among the options, so it has the highest boiling point. Boiling point generally increases with increasing molecular weight and decreases with branching.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1175.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis of oils and fats is called saponification. It produces glycerol and soap (carboxylate salts).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1176.explanation: Ethylene oxide reacts with acidic methanol to give 2-methoxyethanol (CH3OCH2CH2OH). Methanol opens the epoxide ring to give a product with both ether and alcohol functional groups.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1177.explanation: Water has a bent shape with a bond angle of approximately 104.5° (less than 109.5°) because the two lone pairs on oxygen repel each other and the bonding pairs, compressing the O-H bonds closer together.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1178.explanation: Ethers (CH3OCH3 and CH3CH2OCH2CH3) have no O-H or N-H bonds, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other (they only have lone pairs but no hydrogen bond donors). The other pairs have O-H, S-H, or O-H bonds and can hydrogen bond.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1179.explanation: CH4 (methane) has the lowest molecular weight and weakest intermolecular forces (only van der Waals), so it has the lowest boiling point. The chlorinated compounds have higher molecular weights and dipole-dipole interactions, increasing boiling points.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1180.explanation: When both N and S are present, sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN) forms. This gives a blood-red color with FeCl₃, which can be mistaken for a positive nitrogen test.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1181.explanation: Bromine gives a pale yellow precipitate of AgBr, which is partially soluble in concentrated ammonia but less soluble than AgCl.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1182.explanation: Peroxyacids (e.g., mCPBA, peroxyacetic acid) add an oxygen atom to an alkene to form an epoxide via a concerted mechanism.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1183.explanation: NH3 (ammonia) has a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen and is a nucleophile, not an electrophile. Br+, AlCl3 (Lewis acid), and NO2+ are all electron-deficient and act as electrophiles.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1184.explanation: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by the same magnitude but in opposite directions (one clockwise, one counterclockwise). This is the defining property of enantiomers.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1185.explanation: Methane is the primary component of natural gas and is an organic hydrocarbon (contains C-H bonds).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1186.explanation: The 'Structure and Bonding' table (Slide 10) lists 'White' and 'Grey' as allotropes for Tin. Slide 13 further details the interconversion between White tin and Grey tin.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1187.explanation: Bond formation is an exothermic process, meaning energy is released. Bond breaking requires an input of energy (endothermic). A sigma bond is formed by the overlap of atomic orbitals. A carbanion is negatively charged.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1188.explanation: The phenyl group is a benzene ring substituent.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1189.explanation: Amines, especially low molecular weight ones, have characteristic unpleasant odors resembling rotten fish or ammonia.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1190.explanation: Bromination of benzene requires a Lewis acid catalyst like Fe (or FeBr3) to generate the electrophile Br+. UV light is not used for electrophilic aromatic substitution (it would cause free radical addition).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1191.explanation: Benzene reacts with acetic anhydride in the presence of AlCl3 (Friedel-Crafts acylation) to give acetophenone (C6H5COCH3).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1192.explanation: sp² hybridized atoms have an unhybridized p orbital that can participate in π bonding and resonance delocalization, as seen in benzene and conjugated systems.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1193.explanation: The nitro group is a meta director. Bromination of nitrobenzene gives m-bromonitrobenzene. The bromine substitutes at the meta position relative to the nitro group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1194.explanation: Page 4 states, 'Its compounds are more covalent than ionic.' It also notes that its oxide is amphoteric, not basic, and page 5 mentions it forms complexes more readily.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1195.explanation: Chloroform (CHCl3) undergoes oxidation in the presence of light and air to form phosgene (COCl2), a highly poisonous gas. The reaction is: 2CHCl3 + O2 → 2COCl2 + 2HCl.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1196.explanation: PCC is a mild oxidizing agent that stops oxidation at the aldehyde stage for primary alcohols.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1197.explanation: Conjugated double bonds are those on adjacent atoms with alternating single and double bonds (e.g., C=C-C=C), allowing electronic interaction.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1198.explanation: The document states, 'The tetrachlorides are simple covalent molecules with a tetrahedral shape and exist as liquids at room temperature and pressure.' It also notes they are 'non-polar' as a whole.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1199.explanation: Acetic anhydride is obtained by heating acetic acid with a dehydrating agent like P2O5 (phosphorus pentoxide), which removes water and forms the anhydride.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1200.explanation: α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose are anomers that differ in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C-1). They are not mirror images (that would be enantiomers).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1201.explanation: Page 24 explicitly states: 'Na₂SO₃ reacts with powder sulphur (S) to yield sodium thiosulphate (Na₂S₂O₃)' and provides the reaction: 'Na₂SO₃(aq) + S(s) → Na₂S₂O₃(aq)'. It then lists: 'Sodium thiosulphate is useful in photograghy and in iodine titrations.'

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1202.explanation: Free rotation around carbon-carbon sigma (single) bonds allows different spatial arrangements (conformations).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1203.explanation: Page 22 notes, 'PbO₂ decomposes to PbO and O₂ above 300 °C'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1204.explanation: Lindlar’s catalyst hydrogenates alkynes to cis‑alkenes by syn addition without further reduction to alkanes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1205.explanation: Acetonitrile (CH3CN) is reduced by LiAlH4 to ethylamine (CH3CH2NH2). The nitrile is reduced to a primary amine.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1206.explanation: An electron-rich atom is called a nucleophile, not an electrophile. Electrophiles are electron-poor and seek electrons. The other statements are correct.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1207.explanation: Formaldehyde (HCHO) lacks alpha-hydrogens and undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated NaOH to give methanol (reduction product) and sodium formate (oxidation product).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1208.explanation: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. AlCl3 has an incomplete octet and can accept a lone pair, making it a Lewis acid. Methanol, ammonia, and dimethyl ether are Lewis bases (electron-pair donors).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1209.explanation: α-D-Glucopyranose is a cyclic hemiacetal formed by intramolecular reaction of the aldehyde group with the C5 hydroxyl group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1210.explanation: Tetraethyllead (Pb(C2H5)4) was widely used as an antiknock additive in gasoline to increase octane number and reduce knocking. Its use has been phased out due to environmental concerns.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1211.explanation: Aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution (Cu²⁺ complex) to red/brown cuprous oxide (Cu₂O) precipitate.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1212.explanation: Grignard reagents react readily with both aldehydes and ketones via nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group. Fehling's, Tollens', and Schiff's reagents are specific tests for aldehydes (not ketones).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1213.explanation: Addition follows Markovnikov's rule: H adds to less substituted carbon (terminal), Br adds to more substituted carbon, giving 2-bromopropene (CH3CBr=CH2).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1214.explanation: Freon-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl2F2) is a chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) that was widely used as a refrigerant in air conditioners and refrigerators.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1215.explanation: A three-membered cyclic ether is called an oxirane, also known as an epoxide. The simplest is ethylene oxide (oxirane).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1216.explanation: Epoxides have significant ring strain (about 114 kJ/mol) due to the 60° bond angles in the three-membered ring, making them much more reactive toward nucleophiles than acyclic ethers.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1217.explanation: A Bronsted-Lowry base is defined as a species that accepts a proton (H+). A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1218.explanation: Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to achieve multiple vaporization-condensation cycles, effectively separating liquids with close boiling points (e.g., methanol and ethanol, petroleum fractions).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1219.explanation: Page 13 shows 'White tin (Metallic)' and 'Grey tin (non metallic)' as the two allotropes of Tin, with a transition between them at different temperatures ('cold' for Grey tin, 'heat' for White tin).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1220.explanation: Ozonolysis of 2-methyl-2-butene (CH3-C(CH3)=CH-CH3) gives acetone (CH3-CO-CH3) from the carbon bearing two CH3 groups, and acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) from the carbon bearing one CH3 group.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1221.explanation: H2 is a homonuclear diatomic molecule with no electronegativity difference between the two atoms, making it nonpolar. HCl, CH3Cl, and NH3 are all polar molecules due to electronegativity differences.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1222.explanation: The tertiary carbon undergoes SN1 cleavage, giving tert-butyl bromide and methyl bromide (from the methyl group via SN2).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1223.explanation: Page 6 mentions, 'it is the only alkali metal which can react with nitrogen to form nitride 6Li + N₂ → 2Li₃N'.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1224.explanation: Diamond has an extremely high melting point of about 3500°C due to its strong covalent 3D network.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1225.explanation: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + HC≡CH. This was once an important industrial route to acetylene.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1226.explanation: Gammexane (or BHC, benzene hexachloride) is hexachlorocyclohexane (C6H6Cl6), specifically the gamma isomer. It is an insecticide.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1227.explanation: An sp hybridized carbon forms two sigma bonds, which means it is bonded directly to two atoms. It also forms two pi bonds (as in a triple bond) or two pi bonds to two different atoms (as in an allene).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1228.explanation: CH3(CH2)12CO2H is tetradecanoic acid (myristic acid), a long-chain carboxylic acid, which is a fatty acid.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1229.explanation: In halohydrin formation, Br2 forms a bromonium ion intermediate. Water (H2O) acts as the nucleophile, attacking the more substituted carbon of the bromonium ion to give the bromohydrin (1-bromo-2-butanol).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1230.explanation: Baeyer's reagent is a cold, dilute, alkaline solution of potassium permanganate (KMnO4). It is used to test for unsaturation (alkenes and alkynes) by the disappearance of the purple color.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1231.explanation: The longest chain is three carbons (propanol) with a methyl on carbon 2. Both 2-methyl-1-propanol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are correct.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1232.explanation: Aldehyde has higher priority than alcohol, so suffix -al, OH becomes prefix hydroxy- at carbon 3 (butanal numbering).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1233.explanation: A carbon-carbon triple bond consists of one sigma (σ) bond and two pi (π) bonds. This is the typical structure of alkynes.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1234.explanation: A vicinal dihalide undergoes two successive E2 eliminations with a strong base like NaNH₂ to form an alkyne.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1235.explanation: Anisole (C6H5OCH3) on heating with concentrated HI undergoes cleavage to give phenol (C6H5OH) and methyl iodide (CH3I).

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1236.explanation: Organic compounds are primarily covalent, not ionic. The other options (low melting points, low water solubility, and poor conductivity) are characteristic properties of organic compounds.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1237.explanation: 2-Propanol (isopropyl alcohol) gives a positive iodoform test (yellow precipitate of CHI3) because it has the CH3-CHOH- group. 1-Propanol and 1-butanol do not, and 2-methyl-2-propanol (tertiary) also does not.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1238.explanation: Page 10 states: 'With the exception of lithium which reacts slowly, group 1 metals react violently with water to give the corresponding hydroxide and liberate hydrogen gas.' It also mentions: 'The hydroxides of group 1 metals are strong bases and are very soluble in water.' and specifically, 'Lithium hydroxide (LiOH) is slightly soluble in water.' Option C correctly captures these details.

uni-unilag-chm102-bank-1239.explanation: NaBH4 selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols without affecting alkenes or esters.
